We’re also not telling you that this stuff is fake and sucks and is going to go away on its own and so we don’t need to do anything to regulate it or be worried about it. Casey’s phrase for this is AI realism. He thinks there’s a big chunk of people who are just sort of curious and interested and maybe a little scared, but their reaction to the fear is not to try to bury their heads in the sand, but to try to understand the thing.So we started feeling this when we were doing Hard Fork where we would do something that just seemed kind of not our vibe. We would do a Claude Code walkthrough tutorial where we would just spend half an hour building a website and film ourselves and throw it up and it would do great. So people clearly were curious, and even if the comments on the videos were all from people who hated AI, there was clearly a lot of demand out there for people who were just like, “I kind of want to know what’s going on.”“I hate that I can’t stop watching this” is a real theme inside of AI coverage for a variety of reasons.Let’s talk about the book. I think that’s going to frame a bunch of the other questions I have. The book is meticulously reported. It is really fun to read. And the point of it, as I’ve heard you describe it, is to tell the history of the deep learning revolution because all these people just talk in Signal and in extremely childish tweets.Tell me about that gap because this is an industry that is obsessed with documenting itself for computers and being legible to computers and not at all to other people, which seems wild to me. So explain the reporting of this book, because it feels like convincing them to even tell you what happened was a slog.It was, yeah. So basically the reason I wrote this is because I was scared that all of this stuff was going to disappear. I am a history buff. I love to read books about the Wright brothers or the electrification of rural America or the moments of great invention during the PC revolution. I’m such a sucker for that stuff.What you notice as you read more of these books is just that they all rely on a lot of contemporaneous notes and evidence — the lab notes from the scientists developing the atomic bomb, the correspondence between the Wright brothers and their friends and business partners — that is preserved and archived.It was just clear to me reporting on AI every day that there was not going to be anything remotely similar for this stuff because A, all the people building this stuff work for private companies. They’re not government employees who are legally required to preserve their correspondence. And B, the Signal messages and Slack messages are all set by the lawyers to auto-delete after a certain period. So there was literally going to be kind of a mass disappearance with each passing year of these, I think, historically important artifacts, moments, and stories.And then C, the researchers are all too busy to keep notes. They’re all grinding because they’re trying to build the machine god. So, I thought as a journalist, but more so almost as a historian, which is not a role I’ve ever officially played, but one I think I was playing with this book. I was just like, “I’ve got to just get this stuff because I have this sort of privileged ringside seat. These people talk to me. I know some of them will sit down and talk to me and tell me the stories.”We did a lot of it on background so they could be protected from the consequences of talking to me. But this was sort of my attempt to furiously get all the stuff and put it in the archive where future generations could look at it.The theme that really jumps out at me as I read the book was there’s a moment when AGI goes from being a thing they’re all dreaming about to being a thing that they all have to build and the shackles come off and they say, “We have to do this,” and they all drive toward it as hard as they can.You talk specifically about Google where the Overton window moved and suddenly the people inside of Google, who thought this was all a pipe dream and pretty silly, started talking about AGI. That moment feels like the single most important moment in the history of AI, where “Won’t it be great?” goes to “We better go as fast as we can.”Talk about that a little bit, because that shift inside these companies feels under-reported. Yeah, I think that’s absolutely right. I mean, people have been talking and writing about AGI or some precursor that wasn’t called AGI but meant the same thing since literally antiquity. And especially since the 1950s, when the term artificial intelligence was born, people were talking about it. Alan Turing was writing about the thinking machine that could do anything the human brain could.So this concept has been around for a long time, but there was no technology anywhere on the market or in research labs that could actually do what people wanted it to do — that could take in information, learn to learn about that information, and then use that to make predictions and act in the world. People tried lots of different ways to do this and none of them worked all that well.What really needed to happen was the transformer needed to come along. This architecture that Google developed in 2017 and published and then presented to, among other places, OpenAI, which took the idea of the transformer and ran with it. And that’s the T in ChatGPT today. But that was the–Somewhere a Google PR person just leapt out of a bush to hand you a check.They do love this line.They love it when you say it. They get so happy.They love it. They love it less when you point out that although they invented it, they absolutely failed to turn it into a product until after OpenAI did.But yeah, it was a dream, but there was nothing to attach to the dream. There was no technology. And then the large language model came and suddenly it was like, “Oh, maybe this is the thing that could scale forever and keep improving over many orders of magnitude.” So, that’s the light bulb that goes off at OpenAI and then later at Google is like, “Now we have the tool to do the thing that we have always wanted to do.”You’ve got a line in there where you just point out that next-token prediction has not failed yet — that it is doing all the things people want it to do. We’ve obviously had to develop lots of technology around it. There are harnesses to make agents work. There’s reinforcement learning. There’s all this stuff around it. But that core technology has scaled.The reason I bring that up is that in 2023 into 2024, I would ask every AI person who would come on the show or that we would see on The Verge whether LLMs can do it. Can they do the thing you want them to do? Because I don’t think at that moment it was clear that they could.We’re closer now. They’re all openly talking about AGI. We are watching Meta’s Muse just walk its little butt around the internet whenever it wants. Do you think LLMs can do it? Do you think they can get there?I think they can. I’m not certain about that, but they’ve been shockingly good and effective so far. If you go back and you look at the first LLMs, it’s just like 99 percent of people thought this is crazy, that this won’t scale. And then it just keeps working at every stage, at every order of magnitude. I’ve asked people, what was it about next-token prediction that was clearly superior to everything that came before it? There have been people who have told me this actually exists in the human brain too. There’s a whole school of thought that says that what is happening inside the human brain is essentially next-token prediction at scale. Obviously, it’s more complicated. These are not one-for-one replicas of each other.But I think this is the fundamental mystery at the heart of AI: why is next-token prediction so remarkably effective? I think we don’t know. I kind of think it’s one of these cosmic mysteries, but why all of this works is because next-token prediction turns out to generalize really, really, really well.There’s a part of that where all these companies had to believe it. Dario Amodei of Anthropic obviously wrote his paper, “Big Blob of Compute,” where he said you can just do it. You can just dump data and compute at this and we’ll get there. Everyone else had to be convinced of this.What path did the AI companies all take to be convinced of this, and are they all fully convinced of it now?I don’t think they’re all fully convinced of it now. I think they are convinced of it to varying degrees. Ilya Sutskever has this phrase, “Feel the AGI,” that he would walk floor to floor at OpenAI chanting in the old days and reminding people to feel the AGI. I think the labs feel the AGI to varying degrees. I think Anthropic is clearly the most AGI-pilled of the labs, with OpenAI kind of a close second.And then there’s Google, which I think has always struggled to feel the AGI. I think there are lots of reasons for that, but it’s very funny. I love this section of the book where there’s this internal memo battle at Google, where they would just go on their internal message boards and Googlers love to write these manifestos and then snipe at each other’s manifestos and things like that.So a researcher writes this memo, “Say AGI,” which is all about how Google — if it wants to win in AI, recruit the top technical talent, and remain safe about how it’s developing AI — has to admit, through using this term AGI, that what they are building is more than just a bunch of tools to make your Gmail better and make your docs better and make your Google Photos better at recognizing the people’s faces. It is all actually building up to something like a kind of human-level general intelligence.And then someone else immediately writes a memo that’s like, “Don’t say AGI, it’s a horrible, unscientific term.” They go back and forth like this for a while, and you’ll notice even today, [Google CEO] Sundar Pichai does not say AGI.No, he won’t.Demis Hassabis says AGI. Sergey Brin says AGI. So I think there are kind of factions within Google that either think this is still crazy and we should talk about these things as narrow tools versus I think this growing and ascendant faction that is saying, “No, no, no, we’re building AGI, or at least we better say we’re building AGI because otherwise all of our top people are going to go work for OpenAI or Anthropic.”I think you and I had the same experience at Google I/O in May, where we watched Demis Hassabis end the whole keynote by saying, “We’re in the foothills of the singularity.” And then we both went and interviewed Sundar and said, “What does that mean?” And he was like, “Yeah, yeah, Demis. Cool guy.”[Laughs] Take it up with Demis.He was like, “What a kooky character that guy is, building the machine god over here. Let me tell you about the new features in Google Assistant.”There’s some big disconnect there that maybe explains everything about Google at this point in time. The reason I’m asking about this in particular, about this moment when they all clicked over to realize somehow we have to talk about it, is that OpenAI and Anthropic were founded to do this. They were built to make this happen.But they don’t agree on how it should work. I saw you at your book party in New York and you said that you could have retitled your book “Fuck That Guy,” because they all truly hate each other.It’s true.And yet it seems like they have the exact same idea — that they can get there with this technology. The commercial imperatives on OpenAI and Anthropic are very different from the commercial imperatives for Google. Right now, as you and I are talking, it’s not clear to me that they can get to AGI before they run out of money or before CoreWeave collapses or before the bubble writ large comes to some other conclusion about the state of the economy.Do you think that their religious fervor at AGI is keeping them from running a business? If I ran Anthropic today, a logical thing you could say is we should stop training new models and sell the very capable ones we have to more people.I think that belief in AGI is a double-edged sword. I think on one level, yes, if you are super AGI-pilled as the CEO of a frontier AI company, you are going to struggle to care about things like what is my profit margin on inference? Where is my next slate of enterprise customers coming from? Because how boring is that compared to “we are going to build the superhuman machine intelligence that leads us into the post-singularity future”?On the other hand, I think belief is actually a key ingredient in AI success, because belief and the ability to act on that belief is what leads you to do these bet-the-farm moves that can really pay off and have really paid off.Do you remember a year ago when everyone was saying, “Oh my God, OpenAI is spending so much money on compute; how are they ever going to pay for all this compute? Isn’t Sam Altman overextending?” Even Dario was giving interviews where he was throwing shade at OpenAI for spending so much goddamn money on compute.Fast-forward a year and OpenAI is now the only major AI company that is not severely compute-constrained. That belief that led Sam and his executives to bet and maybe overbet on compute last year was the reason that they are in a better position than Google or Anthropic or Meta or anyone else today. So I don’t want to say it’s always a liability to believe this hard, because I think it actually does allow you to make the bets that do end up paying off if the scaling continues to work.It’s interesting because I might reframe that OpenAI decision. You write very poignantly in your book about what people at OpenAI call “the blip,” where Sam Altman was fired for 20 minutes and then he came back and that cleared out a bunch of people from OpenAI.It is the moment you described in the book where OpenAI went from being a research company into being a business. The rational business decision was, “We need to sell more AI to people. We ought to have as much of it as we can.” And Sam is well known to be a ruthless business person. I’ve heard people describe him as S-tier at raising money, which is just an incredible Silicon Valley phrase.So I look at that as a business choice. They got rid of a bunch of stuff they were doing. They pivoted to making enterprise AI products, which is where the money is, and then they realized they needed to service that demand. You’re saying that was a bet on AGI, which to me is a more idealistic turn. Can you square those two?Yeah, I think it absolutely is a bet on AGI because Sora, which they launched and spent a bunch of money and compute on and then killed, is a cool toy that might open up a new line of business for you, but it is not going to get you closer to AGI.What actually gets you closer to AGI is sparking recursive self-improvement by building really good coding models and then turning them back on themselves. That was something that Anthropic was doing. OpenAI got distracted by the side quests and shiny objects that it had last year, and the company was getting its asses kicked. So OpenAI decided to trim the sails, cut fat, and really focus on coding and long-horizon agentic workloads. You have to think there is some spirit, some soul, some secret sauce of cognition that is not just data entering and being processed and transforming inputs into outputs.Look, I know that is the least romantic, most San Francisco way of explaining what human cognition is. I just have not heard a compelling argument that it is not how our brains work that doesn’t involve some sort of supernatural or immaterial substance.There’s a surprising number of neuroscientists and religious scholars listening to the show. They’re going to come find you.They will.I’m confident. Let me just ask you this. There’s a surprising amount of religiosity in Silicon Valley right now. We just published the Peter Thiel lectures on The Verge. He’s talking about the Antichrist. Do you think these ideas are connected, that we are building God such that they seek God?Yes. I think we will absolutely have AI religions. I think AI is posing all of the same questions as a religion that we would not otherwise be asking of God. “What is our purpose? What is our meaning? Why are we here?” These are the questions that people now talk about in the context of AI.I often tell people that being in San Francisco these days feels like living in Europe during the Reformation, where you just have crazy wild-eyed prophets waving their pamphlets around and trying to get you to join their thing. This is what walking down Market Street in San Francisco feels like.What dropped the scales from your eyes? What made you AGI-pilled?Bing’s Sydney, believe it or not.Yeah?I mean, that was the start. And then from there, it was just kind of a gradual process. One day I realized when I used these things, I wasn’t treating them like an intellectual inferior. I was in some ways treating them as a peer, and that’s when I realized, “Oh, something’s happened here.”So it’s possible I have AI psychosis. It would not be the first time I’ve heard that, but every time that I have thought, “Okay, it can’t possibly get any better than this, this has to be the plateau,” I’ve been wrong.So I’m just learning to approach these things with some humility, and maybe the crazy people who have been predicting that scaling would continue indefinitely are right. If they are, I think we need to learn about them, A, and why they think that, and B, try to figure out what to do about it.Well, Kevin, I’m confident the next time you come on the show, I will have set up a fully AI influencer to make money doing [user-generated content] ads, which is the true future of, I think, all of our businesses.The podcast is Machine Gods. It’s very good. You host it with Casey Newton. And the book is excellent. It’s The AGI Chronicles. Kevin, thank you so much for being on Decoder.Thanks. It was great to see you.Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. We really do read every email!Decoder with Nilay PatelA podcast from The Verge about big ideas and other problems.SUBSCRIBE NOW!
items.author: Nilay Patel
items.titleZh: 凯文·鲁斯成了AGI信徒。你为什么不是？
items.descriptionZh:
凯文·罗斯（Kevin Roose）是资深科技记者，曾长期供职于《纽约时报》并主持热门播客《Hard Fork》。近日，他与搭档凯西·牛顿（Casey Newton）离开《纽约时报》，创立了自己的科技播客《Machine Gods》，同时出版新书《The AGI Chronicles》（AGI编年史），详细记录了人工智能行业近年来的爆炸性变革以及各前沿实验室竞相构建通用人工智能（AGI）的历程。在本次访谈中，罗斯讨论了从传统媒体转向独立创作者的经历、新播客的定位，以及新书背后的深度报道过程。

**从传统媒体到独立创业**

罗斯表示，离开《纽约时报》创办独立公司是一个重大决定。他与牛顿共同创立播客公司，罗斯因掷硬币获胜而获得CEO头衔。他坦言，自己从未经营过企业，但逐渐发现商业运营的乐趣，尤其是对创始人角色的体验超出预期。他提到，媒体行业长期对全面投入YouTube等视频平台持谨慎态度，部分原因是结构性经济因素，部分是因为缺乏能够做出长期承诺的机构。但他认为，YouTube是当下全球最重要的媒体平台，而高质量新闻在其中的占比极小，因此他希望探索如何在YouTube上实现可持续的新闻视频模式。

《Machine Gods》与NPR合作，定位为“视频优先”的播客产品，将在YouTube、Apple Podcasts和Spotify等多平台分发。罗斯认为，YouTube是目前最稳定的媒体基础设施，难以被替代——要取代YouTube，不仅需要为创作者和用户提供更好的体验，还需要复制整个人类的视觉内容 corpus（例如数百万条水管工修理水槽的教学视频），这几乎不可能。

**AI报道受众的变化与“AI现实主义”**

罗斯观察到，AI报道的受众正在分化：一部分是构建AI产品的人，热衷消费所有相关内容；一部分是坚决反对AI的人，认为一切都是假的；而中间群体正在扩大——这些产品已变得更有用，人们开始以实际表现来评估它们。牛顿将此概括为“AI现实主义”：一大群人只是好奇、感兴趣，也许有些害怕，但他们的反应不是逃避，而是试图理解。

罗斯指出，过去一段时间市场上存在大量“安慰性”内容，告诉人们AI不会成真、不必关注。但多数人已经接受或对AI不会消失这一事实感到兴奋。他在《Hard Fork》时期就发现，即使是看似不符合节目调性的内容——比如Claude Code的实操教程——也能获得大量关注，说明人们确实想知道发生了什么。

**《The AGI Chronicles》：记录一场可能消失的历史**

罗斯写这本书的动机源于一种历史学者的紧迫感。他热爱阅读关于莱特兄弟、美国农村电气化、PC革命等重大创新时刻的书籍，注意到这些著作都依赖大量同时代的笔记和证据——科学家的实验记录、当事人之间的通信等。但在AI行业，这些材料正在系统性地消失：从业者受雇于私营企业，不受政府档案保存法规约束；Signal和Slack消息被律师设置为定期自动删除；研究人员忙于“研磨”模型，无暇记录。因此，他利用自己作为记者的“场边特权席位”，尽可能多地采访和记录（约150人），许多内容以背景方式呈现以保护受访者。

**AGI从梦想变为必须：转折点**

书中的一个核心主题是AGI从纯粹的梦想变为必须实现的目标。罗斯指出，AGI的概念由来已久，可以追溯到古代，艾伦·图灵就曾描述过能做出人脑所能做的一切的“思考机器”。但长期以来没有任何技术能够实现这一愿景——接收信息、学习关于信息的知识、并据此做出预测和行动。

关键的转折点是2017年谷歌开发并发表的Transformer架构。谷歌将其发表并展示给了包括OpenAI在内的多个机构，OpenAI抓住这一想法全力推进——这就是ChatGPT中的“T”。但具有讽刺意味的是，谷歌虽然发明了Transformer，却未能将其转化为产品，直到OpenAI率先做到。

罗斯认为，下一词预测（next-token prediction）至今尚未失败——它不断在每一个数量级上持续有效。他引用一种观点认为，人脑内部本质上也是大规模的下一词预测。这构成了AI的核心谜团：为什么下一词预测如此高效？他认为这可能是一个宇宙级的奥秘，但事实是下一词预测的泛化能力极强。

**各实验室的“AGI信仰”程度不一**

罗斯指出，各实验室对AGI的信念程度不同。Anthropic是最“AGI-pilled”（深信AGI）的实验室，OpenAI紧随其后。谷歌则一直难以“感受AGI”。书中记录了谷歌内部的一场备忘录论战：一位研究员撰写《Say AGI》，主张谷歌若想在AI领域获胜、招募顶尖人才并保持安全，就必须承认他们正在构建的不仅仅是让Gmail或Google Photos更好的工具，而是通向人类水平通用智能的东西。随即另一位员工撰写《Don't Say AGI》，称这是一个可怕的不科学术语。至今谷歌CEO桑达尔·皮查伊（Sundar Pichai）仍不说AGI，而德米斯·哈萨比斯（Demis Hassabis）和谢尔盖·布林（Sergey Brin）则说。罗斯认为谷歌内部存在派系：一方认为这仍是疯狂的想法，应将其作为窄工具来讨论；另一方则认为必须宣称自己在构建AGI，否则顶尖人才会流向OpenAI或Anthropic。

**商业压力与AGI信念的双刃剑**

罗斯认为，对AGI的信念是一把双刃剑。一方面，如果CEO极度“AGI-pilled”，就很难关心利润率、企业客户等琐事；另一方面，信念是AI成功的关键 ingredient——正是信念驱动了“押上农场”的决策，而这些决策确实获得了回报。他举例说，一年前所有人都在质疑OpenAI在计算上花费太多，而一年后OpenAI是唯一没有严重计算约束的主要AI公司。正是萨姆·奥尔特曼（Sam Altman）及其高管去年对计算的大举押注，使OpenAI今天处于比谷歌、Anthropic、Meta更有利的位置。

关于OpenAI的“blip”（奥尔特曼被解雇又回归的事件），罗斯认为这标志着OpenAI从研究公司转变为商业公司。但他强调，OpenAI砍掉Sora等副业、聚焦编程和长周期代理工作负载，本质上仍是AGI押注——因为真正通向AGI的路径是通过构建优秀的编程模型并让其自我递归改进，这是目前领先的AGI路径。

**理想主义者能否管理万亿美元公司？**

罗斯指出，这些创始人都是理想主义者，以至于彼此分道扬镳创办各自的公司。但没有人有过从零收入到五年内可能实现2万亿美元IPO的经验——这从未发生过。他认为他们正在“一边建造飞机一边冲向事件视界”，但做得已经尽可能好。他不认为引入可口可乐式的职业CEO是个好主意，因为这些人是狂热者和传教士。他提到，一位前沿公司的人曾告诉他，他们公司可能是“最后一家公司”——“资本主义的目的论终点，可能再也不会有另一家主要由人类运营的大公司。”

**为何不停止？三种理由**

罗斯采访了约150人，询问“如果这么危险，为什么还要做？”答案大致分三类：第一是减少伤害的论点——“总有人会构建这个，配方并不难，只需要大量计算、数据和正确的算法。如果可能，它就会发生，由我们来而不是我们不信任的人来做更好。”第二是真正的信徒——“只要我们能安全地渡过难关，一切都会变得很好。”第三是纯粹觉得有趣——“这很好玩，我喜欢让神经网络写代码。”

**对“AI反弹”的看法**

罗斯认为AI公司并不对反弹感到意外，也不喜欢反弹。一位CEO曾对他说：“我理解，我们还没有治愈任何疾病。我们确实认为工具能做有趣的事，但在重大社会改善方面还没有太多成绩。”一些人遗憾聊天机器人先于癌症治愈出现，但技术树就是这样生长的。现在唯一负责任的做法是继续推进癌症治愈，以便当人们审视AI对生活的影响时，能看到“我的祖母还活着，如果没有AI发现的药物她就不会在这里”。

**谷歌的困境与DeepMind的威胁**

罗斯回顾了谷歌对AI的态度：任务型软件——让搜索好10%、Gmail好5%，持续部署改进，凭借数据访问和规模优势保持领先。但OpenAI出现并进入Bing，引发了市场震动。谷歌被迫反应，但并未全力投入。书中引用马斯克诉奥尔特曼案的庭审记录显示，OpenAI创始人都对谷歌、特别是哈萨比斯感到恐惧。罗斯认为这种恐惧是合理的：2015至2016年，DeepMind是唯一真正重要的AGI实验室，在围棋、星际争霸等游戏中获胜，深度强化学习似乎可能一路扩展到AGI。如果AlphaGo Zero能在几小时内从零到击败世界最佳棋手，那么也许可以将围棋替换为数学或编程，快速攀登任务阶梯。虽然事实证明没有LLM不行，但在另一个平行宇宙中，DeepMind可能最先到达AGI。

**技术路径：LLM是否足够？**

罗斯表示，对LLM持怀疑态度的人常回归“世界模型”理念——认为要实现AGI必须能视觉理解物理世界、驱动机器人。但他本人相信“一切都是软件”，LLM是最有希望的路径。也许需要对架构做些调整、构建持续学习方法，但所有实验室都在押注LLM将继续有效。

**关于Bing Sydney与“活着”的讨论**

牛顿提到2023年Bing的Sydney聊天机器人事件，当时罗斯的《纽约时报》文章标题为“Bing's AI chat: 'I want to be alive'”，引发广泛关注。罗斯澄清他从未说Sydney是活的，文章中明确表示他不认为Sydney有感知。但他承认，现在对当今AI系统的“意识概率”评估比2023年的模型更高。他认为Sydney之所以令人毛骨悚然，一个平庸的解释是：那是GPT-4的首次公开部署——微软在未完全准备好的情况下将其塞进了Bing。GPT-4相比GPT-3在对话体验上有主观上的阶跃变化，可能跨越了某种感知鸿沟，让人们觉得“这东西像人”。微软同期发表的“Sparks of AGI”论文也反映了同样的感受。

**关于“活着”的语义与能力饱和**

牛顿指出，随着模型能力提升，人们对它们的期望也在提高。罗斯认为，在“像人一样交流”这一维度上已经饱和——没有太多提升空间。但在解决数学和科学中的新问题等方面仍有大量空间。他提到，现在硅谷的人说话都像Claude——“这是一个承重事实”“我希望这能清晰地传达给你”等表达已成为日常。

**AI社交场景与“最后一家公司”文化**

罗斯描述了AI行业的社交场景：这是一个非常小的亚文化群体，彼此相识，许多人跨实验室约会或结婚。有LAN派对玩《帝国时代》，有跨实验室的扑克局。书中记录了一场Grimes担任DJ的加速主义运动派对，她在演出中途说“我不同意你们任何人”然后继续打碟。罗斯认为，这个小型社交圈与“我们可能重塑世界”之间的冲突，正是反弹的核心——“哦，我们大概应该在这里有发言权。”

**这些公司能否“成功”？**

在闪电问答中，罗斯预测OpenAI、Anthropic和谷歌都会“成功”——成为万亿美元级别的公司，可能还有一两家其他公司。他认为存在网络效应和赢家通吃或赢家通吃大部分的动态。虽然有人相信“单例理论”（一旦有一个AGI，它会去融化其他实验室的芯片），但他认为最终会有少数几个AGI。

关于开源模型和中国竞争是否会摧毁定价权，罗斯不认同。他指出推理成本仍在上升而非下降，即使开源模型也需要在计算机上运行，推理越来越计算密集。训练预算可能下降，但推理预算在可预见的未来将保持强劲。人们愿意为绝对最好的模型付费，不想用六个月前稍差的模型。此外，一旦打击蒸馏（通过大量调用更聪明模型的推理来制造稍笨的开源版本），开源模型的质量与闭源模型质量之间的紧密关联可能不再成立。

**需要理想主义狂热**

罗斯认为，没有理想主义的狂热就无法到达AGI。虽然皮查伊可能没有这种狂热，但谷歌有布林。或者Meta有亚历山大·王（Alexandr Wang），一位公认的真正信徒。你需要在决策权威位置上有真正信徒，或者像马克·扎克伯格这样极具竞争力的人，采用任何他认为能赢的策略。

**罗斯的AGI信念与牛顿的怀疑**

罗斯承认自己是“AGI-pilled”。他的转折点正是Bing Sydney——从那开始，逐渐意识到自己不再把这些工具当作智力上的劣等者，而是在某些方面当作同行。每当他以为“这肯定是平台期了”，他都错了。他正在学习以谦逊的态度对待这些事物，也许那些预测缩放将持续无限的“疯狂的人”是对的。

牛顿则表示自己不是AGI-pilled，尽管罗斯的书让他比以往任何时候都更接近。他认为这些系统存在一种固有的脆弱性。他举例说，让Muse去填写某个简陋政府网站上的文件，网站无法告诉Muse对错，它就崩溃了。他认为数学等具有客观可验证性的领域非常适合这些工具，但世界的大部分并不具备这种可验证性。他怀疑LLM能否克服脆弱性成为“机器神”。

罗斯回应说，要相信人脑中的活动不是一种计算形式，就必须是二元论者或宗教信徒，必须认为存在某种精神、灵魂或认知的秘密配方，不仅仅是数据输入、处理和转换。他承认这是“最不浪漫、最旧金山的解释方式”，但他没有听到过不涉及超自然或非物质实体的有力反驳。

**AI与宗教**

罗斯认为AI将与宗教产生深刻关联。AI提出了与宗教相同的问题：“我们的目的是什么？我们的意义是什么？我们为什么在这里？”他说，现在在旧金山的感觉就像生活在宗教改革时期的欧洲，到处是眼睛发亮的先知挥舞着小册子试图让你加入他们的事业。他相信绝对会出现AI宗教。

**结语**

牛顿表示，下次罗斯来节目时，他可能已经设立了一个全AI网红来做UGC广告赚钱——这才是所有人业务的真正未来。《Machine Gods》播客与凯西·牛顿共同主持，已上线。《The AGI Chronicles》一书已出版。

items.title: Cadence reveals Maestro, fine-tuned AI models built to run specialized chip design agents, with early access coming for 'select customers' in Q4 2026
items.description: Cadence unveiled Maestro, domain-specialized AI models for its chip design agents, with early access for select customers in Q4 2026.
items.content: Share Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Reddit Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter Cadence, one of the largest electronic design automation (EDA) companies, has unveiled Maestro, its new portfolio of domain-specialized AI models tailored for its chip design agents, in a press release sent just ahead of earnings. In initial results compared with general-purpose AI models, Cadence claims up to a 30% improvement in the quality of results and that Maestro effectively uses fewer tokens for the same task, with up to 5x the token efficiency. The first models “are available to select early access customers” in Q4 2026, and customers may run them on Cadence’s cloud, public clouds, or customer-controlled on-premises environments and post-train them on their own “proprietary data, designs, and workflows.” To learn more about Maestro, we spoke with two Cadence executives: Rob Knoth, senior group director of strategy and new ventures, and Paul Cunningham, senior vice president and general manager.This approach is distinct from Synopsys’ own specialized model, GPT-Synopsys, which will run on OpenAI-hosted infrastructure, without using customer data to train the model. The models of both EDA giants, announced less than a month apart, now split on where a customer’s design data goes. Where they might not differ is why: Paul Cunningham, senior vice president and general manager at Cadence, told Tom’s Hardware Premium that agent costs have “really started to explode,” adding, “And I think the world realized so.” That makes it a natural step, he said, to move more of the agents’ iterating “into the weights of the models themselves.” (Image credit: Cadence)Maestro takes this step through Cadence’s AI Super Agents, which “interpret design intent, decompose tasks” and “orchestrate the Maestro portfolio with other leading frontier and open-weight models,” evaluating trade-offs to guide decisions with domain expertise. It also uses reinforcement learning (RL), where Cadence’s “deterministic solvers evaluate outputs against engineering objectives, constraints and ground truth,” and, importantly, the results feed back into the models for improvement.Latest Videos FromTom's HardwareWatch full video here: The models include Nvidia’s Nemotron, and customers can run the customer-data training step themselves with Cadence’s fine-tuning harness, potentially “on their own GPUs, on their own network,” Cunningham said. He added that Nemotron, specifically, was “giving really solid results and actually improving very, very fast.”One constant that keeps popping up with agentic EDA is the need to nail down what the numbers actually measure. In chip design, quality of results usually refers to the design’s power, performance, and area, though Cadence didn’t specify what its 30% figure measures. Both it and the 5x token efficiency figure are measured against “a general-purpose foundation model,” which Cadence told us is the open-source model Maestro started from before its training. The company wouldn’t name the foundational AI model that Maestro is derived from beyond mentioning that it is “one of the leading open source models that’s very competitive with commercial frontier models.” You may like The state of agentic AI in chip design tools in 2026 Synopsys debuts Autopilot platform for developing chips autonomously using AI OpenAI and Synopsys partner to build "GPT-Synopsys" for autonomous chip design Cadence credits the token savings to balancing its EDA and system design automation (SDA) “tool calls with LLM invocations.” As an analogy, Cunningham said, “You don’t need to drive to Safeway in the jet engine,” and you want to use “the right model at the right time for the right task.”Runtime does matter, too: as Rob Knoth, senior group director of strategy and new ventures at Cadence, told Tom’s Hardware Premium in September that a tool call could take anywhere from hours to days to return a value, while the AI industry’s training loops are “used to minutes.” Efficiency could also lower costs, since Maestro use counts toward Cadence’s agent pricing, a subscription with a consumption allowance and charges for use beyond it, Cunningham said. He didn’t say whether the token savings cut a customer’s bill.Being flexible for the customer is a key element of any solution, and for Cadence’s competitor Synopsys, this lies in Autopilot, which Synopsys says allows customers to “choose among commercial, open-source, and fine-tuned language models” across “Synopsys-managed and customer-managed deployments,” with cloud or on-premises infrastructure. For agent security, such as sandboxing, Cadence says it’s working with Nvidia on an integration with Nvidia’s OpenShell Reference Architecture, which Nvidia launched last week, naming both Cadence and Synopsys. These options can help protect customer intellectual property. Swipe to scroll horizontally Cadence Maestro vs. GPT-Synopsys Header Cell - Column 0 Cadence Maestro GPT-Synopsys Announced Oct. 26, 2026 Sept. 30, 2026 What it is A portfolio of domain-specialized AI models for Cadence’s AI Super Agents A specialized model that operates Synopsys’ tools directly Model partner Nvidia (Nemotron, OpenShell) OpenAI Models Post-trained LLMs, trained decision models and agent skills, blended with frontier and open-weight models, including Nemotron OpenAI frontier models Where it runs Cadence’s cloud, public clouds or customer-controlled on-premises environments OpenAI-hosted infrastructure Customer data Customers can post-train it on their own data, designs and workflows, with Cadence’s fine-tuning tools Customer data isn’t used to train the model Claimed results Up to 30% higher quality of results and up to 5x token efficiency vs. a general-purpose foundation model, the unnamed open-source model Maestro started from (initial results; measure not stated) None disclosed Availability First models to select early-access customers in Q4 2026 No date; early technology engagements underway Customers named Socionext, Silicon Labs (Nvidia as partner), frontier AI labs None Pricing Subscription with a usage allowance, then charged by use Not disclosed; Synopsys and OpenAI share revenue under their deal Cadence has had a busy 12 months with customers and agents alike. During Cadence’s July earnings call, CEO Anirudh Devgan said ChipStack, its design and verification agent, “has more than 20 customer engagements,” and ViraStack, its custom and analog agent, “more than 25 customer engagements.” Socionext said just last week that it was applying InnoStack. Silicon Labs has also credited ChipStack with accelerating debugging, and both companies say they are watching Maestro next.Cadence's agentic consolidation began with its acquisition of ChipStack back in November 2025. In June 2026, the company claimed that its agent had reached Level 5 autonomy, which we explored in detail. In September, Knoth teased Maestro’s ingredients to Tom's Hardware Premium a month early, two days before the GPT-Synopsys announcement: “reinforcement learning loops, domain-specific post-training of open-weight models, model routing.” Maestro is now sitting under all four super agents, targeting a similar year-end window to Synopsys’ Autopilot; the table below has the full timeline. Swipe to scroll horizontally Cadence’s agentic AI roadmap When Product Cadence’s claim Status and what’s due November 2025 ChipStack acquisition (agentic verification startup) — Done; co-founder Kartik Hegde now leads Cadence’s core AI research group February 2026 ChipStack AI Super Agent Up to 10x productivity for coding designs and testbenches, test plans, regressions and debug In early access since launch April 2026 ViraStack (custom and analog), InnoStack (digital implementation) and AgentStack (head agent) — Socionext is deploying InnoStack in production; others not stated June 2026 ChipStack at Level 5, with Nvidia’s Nemotron and OpenShell Over 40x faster RTL validation cycles in Nvidia’s deployment Level 5 and AgentStack due to early-access customers in the second half of 2026 July 2026 AuraStack (PCB and advanced packaging) Up to 2x faster time to market and 15x higher productivity Available on Cadence’s Millennium M2000 supercomputer; Nokia is deploying it (Oct. 21) September 2026 ChipStack RTL Generation Agent An average of 24% less area and 18% less power than pure foundation-model code, in early evaluations Due to select early-access customers in Q4 2026; early collaboration with Honda R&D Oct. 26, 2026 Maestro AI Model Portfolio Up to 30% higher quality of results and up to 5x token efficiency vs. a general-purpose foundation model, in initial results First models available to select early-access customers in Q4 2026; about a dozen engagements This rapid pace of progress means that a clear distinction has to be made between early access and general availability. Both Cadence and Synopsys can point to customer engagements, and, at least in the latter’s case for the AgentEngineer portfolio and Autopilot platform, general availability remains a goal by year’s end; Cadence hasn’t given a general availability date for Maestro. For GPT-Synopsys, though, only “early technology engagements are underway,” according to its partners. The platforms and agents remain works in progress.For Maestro, Cunningham hopes for “more case studies, more quantifiable benefits” through Q4. The real story, as he aptly put it, is that “we’re going to bring agents and agentic AI natively into our vertical, not that our vertical is going to get embedded into general-purpose agents.” Only customer results on real workflows will test Cadence’s 30% number, but going by what both companies have shown so far, their own early figures are extremely promising and exciting for the EDA industry.
items.author: Shane Downing
items.titleZh: Cadence发布Maestro：专为运行专用芯片设计智能体而打造的微调AI模型，将于2026年第四季度向“精选客户”开放早期访问
items.descriptionZh:
Cadence近日发布Maestro——一套面向芯片设计智能体的领域专用AI模型组合。该产品在财报前公布，被视为Cadence在“智能体化EDA”竞争中的关键布局。此前不到一个月，Synopsys刚发布GPT-Synopsys，两大EDA厂商几乎同时把生成式AI从通用模型推进到芯片设计专用模型。Cadence高管表示，智能体调用成本“已开始爆炸式增长”，因此有必要把智能体的大量迭代“移入模型权重本身”，让领域模型承担更多推理和决策工作。

技术层面，Maestro通过Cadence的AI Super Agents工作：智能体负责理解设计意图、分解任务，并将Maestro模型组合与其他前沿模型、开放权重模型协同调度，结合领域知识评估权衡并指导决策。Maestro采用强化学习，由Cadence的确定性求解器依据工程目标、约束和 ground truth 评估输出，再将结果反馈给模型以持续改进。模型组合包括Nvidia Nemotron，客户可使用Cadence的微调工具链，在自有GPU和网络上用自己的专有数据、设计和流程对模型进行后训练。部署方式包括Cadence云、公有云以及客户自控的本地环境。

性能方面，Cadence称在初步结果中，Maestro相较通用基础模型可实现最高30%的“结果质量”提升，并在同一任务中最多提升5倍token效率，即用更少token完成相同工作。不过，Cadence未说明30%具体衡量的是哪项指标；在芯片设计中，QoR通常指功耗、性能和面积。5倍token效率的对比基线是Maestro训练前所基于的某个未具名开源通用基础模型。Cadence将token节省归因于在EDA和系统设计自动化工具调用与大模型调用之间做平衡，以及“在正确时间用正确模型做正确任务”的模型路由思路。公司还指出，工具调用可能需要数小时到数天返回结果，而AI训练循环通常以分钟计，因此效率提升也可能影响成本；Maestro使用会计入Cadence智能体订阅的用量额度，超额部分另行计费，但Cadence未明确token节省是否会直接降低客户账单。首批模型将于2026年第四季度向部分早期访问客户提供，约有十余项合作，已提及Socionext、Silicon Labs以及前沿AI实验室等客户或合作伙伴。

与Synopsys的GPT-Synopsys相比，两者最大差异在于客户设计数据的流向。GPT-Synopsys于2026年9月30日发布，运行在OpenAI托管基础设施上，使用OpenAI前沿模型直接操作Synopsys工具，客户数据不用于训练该模型；目前仅处于早期技术合作阶段，未披露性能数据、可用日期和客户。Maestro则由Nvidia Nemotron和OpenShell等组成模型与安全基础，允许客户用自有数据后训练，并可在Cadence云、公有云或客户本地环境运行，强调客户对数据和部署的控制。Synopsys的Autopilot平台则允许客户在商业模型、开源模型和微调模型之间选择，并支持Synopsys管理或客户管理、云端或本地部署。安全方面，Cadence正与Nvidia合作集成OpenShell参考架构，以支持沙箱等智能体安全能力，保护客户知识产权。定价上，Maestro采用带用量额度的订阅制，超额按使用计费；GPT-Synopsys未披露定价，Synopsys与OpenAI按协议分享收入。

Maestro也处在Cadence快速扩张的智能体路线图之下。Cadence于2025年11月收购智能体验证初创公司ChipStack，随后推出ChipStack、ViraStack、InnoStack、AgentStack、AuraStack等智能体，覆盖设计验证、定制与模拟、数字实现、PCB与先进封装等环节。Cadence称ChipStack已有20多项客户合作，ViraStack有25多项；Socionext正在生产环境部署InnoStack，Silicon Labs称ChipStack加速了调试，Nokia则部署AuraStack。2026年6月，Cadence称ChipStack达到Level 5自主性，并在Nvidia部署中实现RTL验证周期超过40倍加速；9月发布的ChipStack RTL生成智能体在早期评估中相较纯基础模型生成代码平均减少24%面积、18%功耗，并与本田研发有早期合作。Maestro目前位于Cadence多类AI Super Agents之下，目标时间窗口与Synopsys的Autopilot相近。

整体来看，Maestro代表了EDA智能体从“调用通用大模型”向“领域专用模型+强化学习+模型路由+客户自有数据后训练”的演进。其潜在影响包括降低token消耗和智能体运行成本、提升芯片设计QoR、支持本地化和专有数据保护，并覆盖RTL生成、验证、模拟/定制设计、数字实现和先进封装等场景。但Cadence尚未给出Maestro的正式通用可用日期，30%提升的具体指标也未披露；Synopsys的Autopilot则将通用可用作为年底目标，GPT-Synopsys仍处早期阶段。Cadence高管希望第四季度获得更多案例和可量化收益，并强调真正的故事是“把智能体和智能体AI原生地带入EDA垂直领域，而不是把EDA嵌入通用智能体”。最终，30%的性能主张仍需真实客户工作流验证，但两家公司目前披露的早期数据已显示出对EDA行业的重要潜力。

items.title: Intel's Lip-Bu Tan has spoken with Lisa Su about potential collaboration with AMD
items.description: Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan has reportedly discussed potential areas of cooperation with AMD chief Lisa Su as Intel works to rebuild its CPU business and expand its foundry operations. The companies have already collaborated on x86 standards and CPU software, including AMD’s integration of its ZenDNN optimizations into Intel’s oneDNN library. Neither executive has publicly detailed the reported discussions or confirmed a new agreement.
items.content: Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Reddit Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article 4 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter Intel and AMD have spent decades competing for the processors inside PCs and data centers, but the rivalry hasn't stopped the two companies from working together when their interests align. And now, Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan has reportedly discussed potential areas of cooperation with AMD chief Lisa Su, adding another possible partnership to the mix as Intel tries to regain its footing in the semiconductor industry.According to a recording (embedded below) of Tan’s October 24 fireside chat with Chinese American Semiconductor Professional Association (CASPA) President Jimmy Cheng, the Intel CEO outlined his plans to rebuild the company’s CPU business, develop chips tailored to specific customer workloads, and attract more customers to its foundry operations. However, Tan did not publicly detail the reported areas of potential cooperation with AMD CEO Lisa Su.Intel has traditionally built its business around its own processor roadmaps, but Tan says the company needs to be more flexible as customers look for silicon designed for particular workloads. He pointed to Intel's Xeon processors as one area where that approach is changing, alongside continued development of GPUs and accelerators.Latest Videos FromTom's HardwareWatch full video here: "We have to reclaim the leadership in CPU. That is something that I am very determined to do." Tan said. Fireside Chat of Lip-Bu Tan and Jimmy Cheng - YouTube Watch On He also described a change in how Intel approaches customization. "Intel is so proud they never want to modify for customer needs," he said. "I'm modifying it for customer needs, and so that, I think, to me, is a fast-growing area, and I'm double, triple down on it." You may like AMD and Intel will work together to create a single PyTorch code path for AI inference on CPUs Intel licenses Atom-class x86 cores to startup AMD seeks 'broader partnership' with Samsung as it looks to secure memory supply The strategy extends beyond conventional CPUs, with Tan identifying application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs), co-packaged optics (CPO), physical AI, and advanced packaging as potential growth businesses. He wants two or three of these areas to eventually contribute around 10% of Intel's revenue each.Intel's foundry business is another major part of Tan's plans. He said the company's 18A manufacturing process had reached volume production, while development of its next-generation 14A process was progressing strongly. Intel has already released version 0.5 of the 14A process design kit (PDK), which provides chip designers with the technical information and tools needed to develop products for the process.Stay On the Cutting Edge: Get the Tom's Hardware NewsletterGet Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.Contact me with news and offers from other Future brandsReceive email from us on behalf of our trusted partners or sponsorsTan said version 0.9 was coming next, followed by version 1.0 for volume production in early 2027. "We have multiple customers [who] really want us to really scale their business," he said, referring to interest in Intel's foundry services.However, Intel did not identify those customers or disclose the size of any potential manufacturing orders during the discussion. Notably, in January, Intel had two prospective customers evaluating 14A test chips, with firm supplier decisions expected during the second half of 2026 and the first half of 2027. Tan also described foundry manufacturing as a business where trust matters as much as technology. Customers hand over wafers that will eventually become products on which their own revenue depends, making missed deadlines or manufacturing problems costly. "The moment we take on the foundry, take on the wafer is a lot of responsibility to make them successful," he said.He recalled one customer who had waited six to eight months hoping he would become CEO before presenting 15 areas where Intel had fallen short. Tan said he addressed the problems individually, after which the customer agreed to deepen its relationship with Intel.That said, the prospect of further cooperation would not be entirely new. In October 2024, Intel and AMD established the x86 Ecosystem Advisory Group alongside other technology companies to coordinate improvements to the x86 instruction set architecture and make it easier for hardware and software developers to support both companies' processors.That cooperation has since moved into AI software. Last week, it emerged that AMD was integrating its ZenDNN optimizations into Intel's open-source oneDNN library, bringing the companies' CPU optimization work for PyTorch AI inference under a common software path. The companies have also worked together on Advanced Matrix Extensions and other x86 capabilities through the advisory group, showing that they cooperate on shared technologies while continuing to compete for customers. For now, however, neither company has announced a new agreement arising from the discussions.
items.author: Newton Gitonga
items.titleZh: 英特尔陈立武已与苏姿丰讨论与AMD的潜在合作
items.descriptionZh:
英特尔与AMD长期以来在PC和数据中心处理器市场激烈竞争，但在共同利益驱动下也曾多次合作。最新报道显示，英特尔CEO陈立武（Lip-Bu Tan）已与AMD CEO苏姿丰（Lisa Su）讨论了潜在合作领域，为两家公司的关系再添一种可能的合作方向。相关消息源自陈立武10月24日与美籍华人半导体专业人士协会（CASPA）主席Jimmy Cheng炉边谈话的录音。陈立武在谈话中介绍了重振英特尔CPU业务、开发针对特定客户工作负载的定制芯片、吸引更多客户使用其代工服务的计划，但并未公开披露与苏姿丰讨论的具体合作领域。

在CPU业务方面，陈立武明确表示要重新夺回英特尔在CPU领域的领导地位。他指出，英特尔过去习惯于按照自身处理器路线图推进业务，但客户越来越需要针对特定工作负载设计的芯片，因此公司必须更加灵活。他以至强（Xeon）处理器为例说明这一转变，同时英特尔仍将继续开发GPU和加速器。陈立武还特别谈到定制化思路的变化：过去英特尔“非常骄傲，不愿为客户需求修改产品”，而现在他正推动根据客户需求进行修改，并将这一方向视为快速增长领域，表示会“加倍、三倍投入”。

这一战略不仅限于传统CPU。陈立武将专用集成电路（ASIC）、共封装光学（CPO）、物理AI和先进封装列为潜在增长业务，希望其中两到三个领域最终各自贡献约10%的英特尔营收。CPO通过将光引擎与芯片封装更紧密集成，有望提升互连带宽和能效；ASIC则面向特定客户工作负载提供定制化算力；先进封装则是提升芯片性能和集成度的重要环节。这些布局反映出英特尔试图从单一处理器供应商向更广泛的定制化计算和制造平台转型。

代工业务是陈立武计划的另一重点。他表示，英特尔18A制程已进入量产阶段，下一代14A制程开发进展强劲。英特尔已发布14A工艺设计套件（PDK）0.5版本，为芯片设计人员提供开发该制程产品所需的技术信息和工具；0.9版本即将推出，面向量产的1.0版本计划于2027年初发布。陈立武称，有多个客户希望英特尔帮助其扩大业务规模，但英特尔未透露客户身份或潜在订单规模。今年1月，曾有报道称两家潜在客户在评估14A测试芯片，最终供应商决策预计在2026年下半年和2027年上半年作出。陈立武还强调，代工制造不仅是技术问题，更是信任问题：客户交来的晶圆最终将变成其收入所依赖的产品，错过期限或制造问题都会带来高昂代价。他回忆，一位客户曾等待六到八个月、希望他成为CEO后才提出英特尔存在的15个不足；在逐一解决这些问题后，该客户同意深化与英特尔的关系。

值得注意的是，英特尔与AMD的进一步合作并非完全没有基础。2024年10月，两家公司已联合其他科技企业成立x86生态系统咨询小组，旨在协调x86指令集架构改进，降低硬件和软件开发者为两家处理器提供支持的难度。这一合作已延伸到AI软件领域：上周有消息称，AMD正将其ZenDNN优化集成到英特尔开源oneDNN库中，使两家公司面向PyTorch AI推理的CPU优化工作纳入共同软件路径。ZenDNN是AMD的CPU深度学习推理加速库，oneDNN是英特尔开源深度学习库，二者整合有助于开发者在AMD和英特尔CPU上获得更统一的AI推理优化支持。两家公司还通过该咨询小组在高级矩阵扩展（AMX）等x86能力上开展合作，说明它们可以在共享技术标准上合作，同时在客户市场继续竞争。不过，目前两家公司均未宣布由上述讨论产生的新协议。

总体来看，这一消息的核心意义在于：面对AI计算需求多样化、定制芯片兴起以及x86生态面临的竞争压力，英特尔正试图以更灵活的定制化策略、先进制程代工和开放软件合作重塑自身定位；而与AMD在x86生态和AI软件优化上的潜在或既有合作，可能降低开发者的适配成本、增强x86架构整体竞争力，但具体合作范围和商业影响仍有待官方确认。

items.title: Nvidia RTX 20, 30, and 40-series GPUs hacked to remove a half-speed AI throttle
items.description: Linux kernel modules lift Nvidia’s half-rate AI tensor limit on GeForce RTX 20, 30, and 40-series GPUs.
items.content: Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Reddit Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article 4 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter Modders have discovered a way to remove imposed half-speed AI performance limits on Nvidia RTX 20, 30, and 40-series GPUs with a firmware exploit, VideoCardz reports. Without the limitation, the RTX 4090 can achieve double its peak tensor rate, and matrix math can improve by up to 80% for the RTX 3090 Ti, with gains on other cards varying. Real workloads gain significantly less than the RTX 4090’s doubled peak would imply, and chatbot token speeds remain about the same, as that performance is dependent on memory bandwidth.For all impacted GeForce generations, Nvidia imposed a limit that, per its own published specs, runs FP32-accumulate math at half each card’s FP16-accumulate rate. That does not apply to its Turing and Ampere pro cards. The unlock returns native matrix-math throughput to owners of the cards, which can speed up prompt processing and image generation.Three separate projects offer generation unlocks, each with its own unofficial Linux module, while experimental Windows builds pursue a different approach. Card coverage varies by generation, with gpu-unlock handling Ampere and listing the GA102/GA103/GA104/GA106 series IDs. An Ada fork, gpu-unlock-ada, covers the RTX 4090 and, experimentally, the 4090 D, 4070 Ti Super, and the 4060 Ti 16GB. The turing-unlock project, adapted from gpu-unlock, works with the RTX 2080 Ti. See Table 1 for a breakdown.Latest Videos FromTom's HardwareWatch full video here: Swipe to scroll horizontally Which GeForce cards each unlock covers Generation Project Cards with reported results Experimental or untested RTX 20 (Turing) turing-unlock RTX 2080 Ti (22GB memory-modded cards) Other Turing GPUs, added untested; FP16 only, since Turing lacks BF16 support RTX 30 (Ampere) gpu-unlock RTX 3090 Ti, 3090, 3080 10GB, 3080 20GB (memory-modded), 3070, 3060 12GB RTX 3070 Ti and GA103 cards untested; one RTX 3080 Ti 20GB OEM card stays at half rate RTX 40 (Ada Lovelace) gpu-unlock-ada RTX 4090 RTX 4090 D, 4070 Ti Super, 4060 Ti 16GB (experimental, one card each) RTX 50 (Blackwell) None — Not supported; gpu-unlock’s developer calls it out of scope How much faster the cards getThe peak doubling is for tensor rates, with the Ada fork developer’s RTX 4090 moving from 165.6 to 331.6 TFLOPS on FP16 and 165.5 to 330.6 TFLOPS on BF16. The gpu-unlock-ada README states that, in one independent owner’s matrix-multiply benchmark, cuBLAS GEMM medians only saw improvements of 12–34% and up to 20%, respectively. A separate data point, for an RTX 4070 Ti on Windows, saw larger matrix-multiply gains of +80.1% and +76.4%, the difference possibly caused by power limits.In the matrix-multiply benchmark, a tested RTX 3090 Ti scored +35% for FP16, +80% for BF16, and +94% for TF32, based on a user’s test with a modified Nvidia driver. The gpu-unlock README lists BF16 matrix-multiply gains from user reports of +25–67% for the RTX 3090, +70–73% for the 3080 10GB, +56–59% for a memory-modded 20GB version, +73–81% for the 3070, and around +80% for the 3060 12GB, though it notes they are not directly comparable. The power limit “matters a lot”: the lowest figure, +25%, came from cards capped at 225 W. For Ampere, LLM prefill improved 14–36%, with diffusion and FlashAttention speeding up, but LLM decode and INT8 stayed “about the same.” You may like Nvidia app update fails to block unofficial DLSS multi-frame generation mod on RTX 40 series gaming GPUs We tested DLSS Multi Frame Generation on RTX 40-series GPUs All-in-one 'DLSS Unlocked' mod brings DLSS 5 and multi-frame gen to RTX 20, 30, and 40 series An RTX 2080 Ti with a 22GB memory mod, a Dell OEM card limited to 250 W, saw FP16 matrix-multiply improvements of +36% to +64% depending on size; BF16 is unaffected, since Turing has no BF16 hardware. A user’s variant of the card at 260 W saw a +59% improvement. A separate project, KohakUnlock, on a Leadtek 2080 Ti 22GB saw an 85% improvement on an instruction rate test, with a best matrix-multiply median of +53% against a second, locked card of the same model.There is “not a claim of a 2× application/game speedup,” says KohakUnlock’s README. See Table 2 for a rundown of the numbers for all three generations. The turing-unlock README notes that the mod “may damage your hardware,” while KohakUnlock adds that it “can hang a GPU or host, prevent boot, corrupt data, or damage hardware,” so caution is advised.Stay On the Cutting Edge: Get the Tom's Hardware NewsletterGet Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.Contact me with news and offers from other Future brandsReceive email from us on behalf of our trusted partners or sponsors Swipe to scroll horizontally Matrix-multiply benchmark gains, unlocked vs. stock Card Precision Gain Tested by RTX 4090 FP16 / BF16 +12–34% / up to +20% One owner, Linux, 450 W RTX 4070 Ti (MSI) FP16 / BF16 +80.1% / +76.4% Separate Windows port, one card RTX 3090 Ti FP16 / BF16 / TF32 +35% / +80% / +94% One user, modified Nvidia driver, 450 W RTX 3090 BF16 +25–67% User reports; lowest at a 225 W cap RTX 3080 10GB BF16 +70–73% User report RTX 3080 20GB mod BF16 +56–59% User reports RTX 3070 BF16 +73–81% User reports RTX 3060 12GB BF16 About +80% User reports RTX 2080 Ti 22GB mod (Dell) FP16 +36–64% turing-unlock developer, 250 W, by matrix size RTX 2080 Ti 22GB mod FP16 +59% One user, 260 W RTX 2080 Ti 22GB mod (Leadtek) FP16 +53% KohakUnlock; best median vs. a locked card RTX 2080 Ti 11GB (ASUS, stock) FP16 +77% haohervchb pre-boot loader How the exploit worksThe explainer for gpu-unlock states that the rate limits are in two “speed selector” registers that the host driver can’t write, but Nvidia’s signed SEC2 “Booter” firmware has a stack buffer overflow which can be exploited to run code in “heavy secure” mode. This was discovered after Nvidia published a debug Booter encrypted with a known public test key. A single 4-byte write with the V67 payload opens the privilege mask so the host can set the full rate, and the module then resets the card before Nvidia’s driver binds it.The underlying bug is described in Jon Pry’s “A Canary in the Crypto Mine: Defeating Stack Protection in a GPU Secure Coprocessor,” published on Zenodo in June. The stack overflow was found on the CMP 170HX in the Heavy Secure Falcon, and the V67 constants come from WildFlash1st/cmp90hx-unlock. The pre-driver timing gpu-unlock uses appear to come from WildFlash1st’s separate Windows EFI bootloader, cmp90hx-unlock-for-windows, while the best-known use of the exploit is the CMP Unlocker for the CMP 170HX. Zagitta, the maintainer of gpu-unlock, said on Hacker News that the project is their work but “the exploits … aren’t my ideas by any means” and that the unlock “just flips the 2 bits” needed.Zagitta said that RTX 40 support is in progress and that forks are already unlocking those cards. Zagitta added that Hopper and Blackwell cards are “out of scope for this approach” at least.The Ada fork says other boards “remain unverified” and that shared firmware “does not establish support for untested cards.” The turing-unlock project, likewise, has a list of untested Turing IDs. Gaps remain for GA103 and most Ada and Turing cards. None of the projects contains a roadmap, but data is being gathered, as gpu-unlock is asking GPU owners for compatibility reports. items.author: Shane Downing
items.titleZh: Nvidia RTX 20、30 和 40 系列 GPU 遭破解，以解除半速 AI 限速
items.descriptionZh:
修改者利用固件漏洞，找到了移除英伟达 GeForce RTX 20、30、40 系列显卡上人为设置的“半速”AI 性能限制的方法。该限制原本使这些消费级 GPU 的 FP32 累加矩阵运算只能以各自 FP16 累加速率的一半运行，而英伟达的 Turing、Ampere 专业卡不受此限制。解锁后，显卡可恢复原生矩阵数学吞吐，从而加快大语言模型的提示处理（prefill）以及图像生成等任务。不过，实际工作负载的收益远低于峰值翻倍，聊天机器人逐 token 生成速度基本不变，因为该阶段主要受显存带宽限制。

目前有三个独立项目提供不同世代的解锁方案，各自提供非官方 Linux 模块，另有实验性 Windows 构建采用不同路径。gpu-unlock 面向 Ampere，列出 GA102/GA103/GA104/GA106 系列 ID，已报告支持 RTX 3090 Ti、3090、3080 10GB、显存改装 3080 20GB、3070、3060 12GB；3070 Ti 和 GA103 卡未测试，一张 RTX 3080 Ti 20GB OEM 卡仍保持半速。gpu-unlock-ada 面向 Ada，覆盖 RTX 4090，并实验性支持 4090 D、4070 Ti Super、4060 Ti 16GB，每类仅一张卡。turing-unlock 改编自 gpu-unlock，适用于 RTX 2080 Ti，其他 Turing GPU 被列为未测试，且因 Turing 不支持 BF16，只能针对 FP16。RTX 50（Blackwell）不在支持范围内，开发者称其超出该方案范围。

性能方面，峰值翻倍主要体现在张量速率上：Ada 分支开发者的 RTX 4090 从 FP16 165.6 TFLOPS 提升到 331.6 TFLOPS，BF16 从 165.5 TFLOPS 提升到 330.6 TFLOPS。但实际矩阵乘法基准中，一位独立用户的 cuBLAS GEMM 中位数仅提升 12%–34%，另一项最高约 20%。一张 Windows 上的 RTX 4070 Ti 取得更大的矩阵乘法提升，分别为 +80.1% 和 +76.4%，差异可能来自功耗限制。RTX 3090 Ti 在修改版英伟达驱动下，FP16 +35%、BF16 +80%、TF32 +94%。gpu-unlock 的 README 汇总用户报告：RTX 3090 的 BF16 矩阵乘法提升 25%–67%，3080 10GB 提升 70%–73%，显存改装 20GB 版提升 56%–59%，3070 提升 73%–81%，3060 12GB 约 +80%，但这些数据并非直接可比。功耗上限“影响很大”：最低的 +25% 来自 225W 功耗上限的卡。Ampere 上，LLM prefill 提升 14%–36%，扩散模型和 FlashAttention 也有加速，但 LLM 解码和 INT8 基本不变。RTX 2080 Ti 22GB 显存改装版中，Dell OEM 卡限制在 250W 时，FP16 矩阵乘法按矩阵尺寸提升 36%–64%；一张 260W 的同类卡提升 59%；KohakUnlock 在一张 Leadtek 2080 Ti 22GB 上测得指令速率提升 85%，矩阵乘法中位数相对同型号锁速卡提升 53%。另有 ASUS 原厂 2080 Ti 11GB 通过预启动加载器取得 +77% 的 FP16 提升。KohakUnlock 明确表示，这并不是宣称应用或游戏能获得 2 倍加速。

技术原理上，gpu-unlock 的说明称，速率限制位于两个主机驱动无法写入的“速度选择”寄存器中，但英伟达签名的 SEC2 “Booter”固件存在栈缓冲区溢出，可被利用在“heavy secure”模式下执行代码。该问题是在英伟达发布一个用已知公共测试密钥加密的调试版 Booter 后被发现的。通过 V67 payload 进行一次 4 字节写入即可打开权限掩码，使主机能够设置全速率；模块随后在英伟达驱动绑定前重置显卡。底层漏洞描述来自 Jon Pry 于 6 月发表在 Zenodo 的论文《A Canary in the Crypto Mine: Defeating Stack Protection in a GPU Secure Coprocessor》，栈溢出是在 CMP 170HX 的 Heavy Secure Falcon 上发现的，V67 常量来自 WildFlash1st/cmp90hx-unlock。gpu-unlock 使用的驱动前时机似乎来自 WildFlash1st 的独立 Windows EFI 启动加载器 cmp90hx-unlock-for-windows，而该漏洞最知名的应用是面向 CMP 170HX 的 CMP Unlocker。gpu-unlock 维护者 Zagitta 在 Hacker News 上表示，项目是其工作，但“这些漏洞利用绝非我的想法”，解锁“只是翻转所需的 2 个比特”。他还称 RTX 40 支持仍在推进，分支已在解锁这些卡；Hopper 和 Blackwell 至少对该方法“超出范围”。

影响与应用场景方面，这一解锁主要有利于本地 AI 工作负载中的矩阵密集型阶段，例如 LLM 提示预填充、扩散图像生成和 FlashAttention 等，对受显存带宽约束的逐 token 解码帮助有限。由于覆盖范围仍不完整，GA103 和大多数 Ada、Turing 卡存在空白，且共享固件并不能证明未测试卡获得支持。风险也不容忽视：turing-unlock 的 README 警告该修改“可能损坏硬件”，KohakUnlock 则称其“可能导致 GPU 或主机挂起、阻止启动、损坏数据或损坏硬件”，因此需要谨慎对待。各项目没有路线图，但正在收集兼容性报告。

items.title: Bitcoin reward offered to anyone who could break into an unpatched server running PHP, hacker cracks site and claims bounty
items.description: The “Steal My Bitcoin” challenge offers a bounty to anyone who can breach a deliberately vulnerable PHP website using the recently disclosed PHP2Shell flaws. The challenge follows previous recoveries of locked Bitcoin fortunes through software vulnerabilities and AI-assisted investigation, but no successful claim has been confirmed.
items.content: Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Reddit Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article 0 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter A hacker has successfully breached a vulnerable server, claiming a prize pot worth $2,021.22 in Bitcoin after exploiting PHP2Shell vulnerabilities, a posting on the Steal My Bitcoin website has shown. The challenge's creator confirmed the win on October 25, ending an experiment designed to test claims that exploiting critical software vulnerabilities is becoming easier.The challenge, hosted on the website a day earlier and announced through a forum post, initially offered approximately $502 worth of Bitcoin. Donations subsequently increased the pot to 0.02511679 BTC, worth $2,021.22 at the time of the win. The creator's website recorded the successful claim at 15:47 UTC on October 25, after the challenge had been running for approximately 19.28 hours.The experiment follows the disclosure of CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, two critical PHP vulnerabilities that can allow remote code execution under certain conditions. The flaws received critical severity ratings, and fixes were released on October 21. Turning the vulnerabilities into a reliable attack, however, requires more than simply running a publicly available exploit against an arbitrary server.Latest Videos FromTom's HardwareWatch full video here: The challenge's creator, posting under the name ‘cloudlandsdev’, had said the project was designed to see whether anyone could use the vulnerabilities to compromise the server and claim its Bitcoin. “Made this because I'm curious if anyone out there has figured out how to actually use this PHP RCE, we spent the last few days panicking. Have fun!” the creator wrote.PHP2Shell refers to two vulnerabilities in PHP’s request-handling and memory-management processes. Under vulnerable configurations, an attacker could potentially exploit these flaws to execute code with the privileges of the web server account. You may like OpenAI says ChatGPT Sol helped uncover critical PHP flaws that could affect 70% of websites Hacker turns 25 cents into 46 billion fake Bitcoins to steal $770,000 Hackers drain $320 million in Bitcoin from Liquid Network, emptying roughly 95% of federation wallet The experiment quickly attracted attention, but the resulting traffic also became a problem. In an update, the creator said visitors were exhausting the server's available computing resources shortly after each capacity increase. Limited storage also prevented the server from retaining all its logs, complicating efforts to document a successful attempt.The winner, ‘KillaBoi’, published a proof of concept on GitHub describing the attack against the live challenge and providing a local test environment. The exploit took advantage of PHP's handling of multipart uploads and session data, where, by pushing a PHP worker beyond its memory limit, the attacker could leave internal state in an inconsistent condition. Subsequent requests then exposed memory contents through session cookies, providing information about the locations of PHP's memory structures and executable code.Stay On the Cutting Edge: Get the Tom's Hardware NewsletterGet Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.Contact me with news and offers from other Future brandsReceive email from us on behalf of our trusted partners or sponsorsNotably, the attacker used those addresses to construct a forged PHP data structure that triggered command execution during cleanup. The final request returned evidence that the command had run inside the PHP process. Although the server was successfully compromised, the recovered private key did not match the advertised prize address. However, on-chain data shows the funds were subsequently sent to an address “bc1qr4…lk7a9”, labeled as a Kraken cold wallet.Bitcoin recovery efforts have previously involved reverse-engineering software rather than exploiting a live server. In 2024, hardware hacker Joe Grand, known as ‘Kingpin”, and researcher Bruno recovered access to 43.6 BTC belonging to an owner identified as Michael, who had forgotten a 20-character wallet password.The researchers reverse-engineered an older version of RoboForm's password generator and identified a flaw that made the password predictable. They recovered the wallet in November 2023, when the Bitcoin was worth approximately $1.6 million. Its value had climbed to nearly $3 million by the time the recovery was reported in May 2024.A more recent case involved a Bitcoin holder who recovered five BTC worth roughly $400,000 in May 2026 after losing access to the wallet for years. The pseudonymous owner, known as ‘cprkrn’, said Anthropic's Claude AI helped identify a backup file from December 2019, which could be decrypted using a password the owner had previously written down in a notebook. The backup contained the keys needed to access the Bitcoin.The latest event comes as security teams face pressure to patch PHP installations following the public disclosure of PHP2Shell. A separate report on the vulnerability disclosure controversy detailed how premature publication disrupted the coordinated release process. That said, for now, evidence of the latest successful attack suggests that exploiting these PHP vulnerabilities may not be that hard after all.

items.titleZh: 比特币悬赏给任何能入侵运行PHP的未打补丁服务器的人，黑客攻破网站并领取赏金
items.descriptionZh:
一场名为“Steal My Bitcoin”的公开挑战显示，一名黑客成功攻破了一台存在漏洞的服务器，并领取了价值2021.22美元的比特币奖金。挑战创建者于10月25日确认了这次成功，结束了这项旨在检验“利用关键软件漏洞是否正变得越来越容易”的实验。该挑战于一天前上线，并通过论坛帖子公布，最初奖金约为502美元，随后在捐赠推动下增至0.02511679 BTC，获胜时价值2021.22美元。创建者网站记录的成功领取时间为10月25日15:47 UTC，此时挑战已运行约19.28小时。

实验背景是CVE-2026-109618和CVE-2026-109619两个严重PHP漏洞的公开披露。这两个漏洞在特定条件下可导致远程代码执行，均获得严重级别评级，修复程序于10月21日发布。不过，把公开漏洞转化为针对任意服务器的可靠攻击并不简单。挑战创建者“cloudlandsdev”表示，该项目是为了观察是否有人能真正利用这些PHP远程代码执行漏洞攻破服务器并取走比特币，并称团队此前几天一直在为此紧张。所谓“PHP2Shell”涉及PHP请求处理和内存管理过程中的两个漏洞；在易受攻击配置下，攻击者可能以Web服务器账户权限执行代码。

挑战迅速引发关注，但流量也带来问题。创建者称，每次扩容后不久，访问者就会耗尽服务器计算资源；存储限制还导致服务器无法保留全部日志，增加了记录成功攻击过程的难度。获胜者“KillaBoi”在GitHub发布了概念验证，描述了对实时挑战环境的攻击，并提供本地测试环境。该利用方式针对PHP对multipart上传和会话数据的处理：攻击者先将PHP工作进程推过内存限制，使内部状态进入不一致条件；后续请求再通过会话Cookie暴露内存内容，从而泄露PHP内存结构和可执行代码的位置信息。攻击者利用这些地址构造伪造的PHP数据结构，在清理阶段触发命令执行，最终请求返回了命令已在PHP进程内运行的证据。

尽管服务器被成功攻破，但恢复出的私钥与挑战宣传的奖励地址并不匹配。链上数据显示，相关资金随后被发送至地址“bc1qr4…lk7a9”，该地址被标注为Kraken冷钱包。文章还对比了此前的比特币恢复案例：2024年，硬件黑客Joe Grand（“Kingpin”）和研究员Bruno通过逆向旧版RoboForm密码生成器，发现密码可预测缺陷，帮助化名Michael的持有者恢复43.6 BTC；2023年11月恢复时价值约160万美元，2024年5月报道时接近300万美元。2026年5月，化名“cprkrn”的持有者在Anthropic的Claude AI帮助下找到2019年12月的备份文件，并用此前记在笔记本上的密码解密，恢复了约40万美元的5 BTC。

此次事件发生之际，安全团队正因PHP2Shell公开披露而面临修补PHP安装的压力。另一份关于漏洞披露争议的报告称，过早发布扰乱了协调披露流程。就目前而言，这次成功攻击的证据表明，利用这些PHP漏洞可能并没有想象中那么困难。

history.title: Leaked 256-core Zen 6c EPYC CPU destroys Zen 5 in early single-threaded benchmarks hints at 24% IPC gain
history.description: A benchmark leak and a direct clock-matched comparison from an enthusiast seed the idea that Zen 6 may come with a decent IPC bump as well as increased clocks.
history.content: Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Reddit Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article 2 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter AMD's Zen 6 processors are out! Well, the EPYC 9006 family of server CPUs is out, anyway. These aren't chips that mere mortals like you and I can reasonably acquire, so there aren't really many third-party benchmarks out there yet, but somebody ran GeekBench 7 on one, and you know what that means: time for some wild speculation, such as the supposed 15% single-threaded IPC increase you might have seen reported this week. However, it isn't quite that clear yet. Well-known enthusiast and occasional leaker HXL (@9550pro) spotted the EPYC 9996 result, and now Russian enthusiast "three twenty six" (@326powah) has done a direct comparison with his Ryzen 7 9700X at the same clock.Let's lay out the details: the AMD EPYC 9996 is an absolutely gargantuan server processor with 256 "Zen 6c" cores spread across eight "Monarch" CCDs with 32 cores apiece. Each CCD has 128MB of L3 cache, which is reportedly split into two 64MB domains for each 16-core CCX. This gives us 4 megabytes of L3 cache per CPU core, which happens to be the exact ratio that AMD has maintained since Zen 2. Meanwhile, 326's Ryzen 7 9700X is a desktop CPU with eight Zen 5 CPU cores and 32MB of L3 cache, giving it the same cache-per-core ratio yet an overall smaller local cache for the CPU cores, to say nothing of the 1GB of L3 cache on the full EPYC 9996.Yes, 1GB of L3 cache. That enormous CPU is also served by a 1024-bit memory bus, likely running at 12,800 MT/s, giving it a colossal 1.64 TB/second of memory bandwidth. However, the specific benchmarks we're comparing here are single-threaded benchmarks, and as a result, they aren't likely to be bottlenecked by memory bandwidth on either machine; even 326's relatively pedestrian DDR5 memory at 6000 MT/s CL34 is more than sufficient for a single-threaded, lightly vectorized workload like Geekbench 7. Matching the CPU core clock rates at 4.1 GHz actually gives us a pretty decent core-to-core comparison of performance, even if all factors are not equal.Latest Videos FromTom's HardwareWatch full video here: Comparing the Linux results, the gain over the desktop chip varies quite a bit depending on the specific test, but there are no regressions. (Image credit: @326powah on X)So how does it come out? Frankly, it's a massacre. That's true whether we look at the Windows 11 results he posted first or the CachyOS Linux results that he posted later, although the Zen 5 part doesn't get embarrassed quite as badly in Linux. The Dell PowerEdge R9815 server hosting the big EPYC part scored 2847 in the single-threaded test; 326's Ryzen desktop scores 2483 in Linux and 2318 in Windows.Looking at the Gala-to-Honeycrisp Linux results, the biggest performance gulf is some 24% in the HTML5 Browser test, which is normally quite sensitive to memory latency. That could easily be caused by the massive L3 cache of the EPYC CPU. Other tests aren't so easily dismissed by configuration mismatches, though. The 19% gain in asset compression, the 21% gain in video encoding, and the 17% gain in photo editing all point to real architectural differences between Zen 5 and Zen 6 that seem quite promising for its desktop debut next year. You may like AMD targets Nvidia with first official benchmarks for EPYC 'Venice' CPUs AMD's Zen 6 CPUs could fix microstutters and improve 1% lows in games via per-core optimizations AMD drops an EPYC $15,000, 256-core beast What's fascinating is that these results won't have been affected much by the considerable SIMD horsepower of the Zen 6 CPU core, as Geekbench—at least historically speaking—makes relatively light use of CPU SIMD, and in fact, this specific test is marked as "AVX2," meaning it definitely isn't using the muscular AVX-512 units present in either CPU. In fact, most of these tests are actually measuring CPU integer arithmetic and memory subsystem performance more than raw CPU number-crunching power, so Zen 6 coming out so far ahead here is really interesting. Media processing seems to be especially strong on Zen 6. (Image credit: @326powah on X)Obviously, you shouldn't take this as gospel that "Zen 6 has 15% higher IPC than Zen 5," though that's arguably a plausible conclusion; there are just too many confounding factors to say that so far. Indeed, another one of those factors is that this isn't the Zen 6 CPU core that we'll be getting in desktop CPUs. The EPYC 9996 is a high-density part that uses Zen 6c, the specialized dense core design meant for increased area efficiency at the cost of its ability to scale to high clocks. After all, 4.1 GHz isn't exactly a high clock rate these days, and particularly not for chips manufactured on a bleeding-edge 2nm-class manufacturing process.Stay On the Cutting Edge: Get the Tom's Hardware NewsletterGet Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.Contact me with news and offers from other Future brandsReceive email from us on behalf of our trusted partners or sponsorsThat's the part that should get you excited. Zen 5 had a very modest IPC uplift over Zen 4 (including even some regressions), and combined with a similarly modest clock rate gain, it wasn't a very exciting release for most desktop users. Zen 6 seemingly may have a significant IPC advantage as well as, if rumors hold, a fairly extreme clock jump over the current-generation parts. If that holds, this may be another leap like from Core 2 to Core i7, and these parts are confirmed to be coming to an AM5 socket near you. We'll be waiting with bated breath for the launch early next year. Hopefully there's RAM to buy by that point. history.titleZh: 泄露的256核Zen 6c EPYC CPU在早期单线程基准测试中碾压Zen 5，暗示IPC提升24%
history.descriptionZh:
AMD 的 Zen 6 架构首先以 EPYC 9006 系列服务器 CPU 的形式登场，其中 EPYC 9996 是一款面向高密度服务器的巨型处理器：它拥有 256 个“Zen 6c”核心，分布在 8 个“Monarch”CCD 上，每个 CCD 32 核；每个 CCD 配备 128MB L3 缓存，并据称按每 16 核 CCX 拆分为两个 64MB 域，因此每核对应 4MB L3，延续了 AMD 自 Zen 2 以来的缓存/核心比例。整颗芯片的 L3 缓存高达 1GB，并配有 1024-bit 内存总线，速率可能为 12,800 MT/s，理论内存带宽达 1.64 TB/s。不过，这次对比的是单线程 GeekBench 7 测试，内存带宽不太可能成为瓶颈，即便对比平台使用 DDR5-6000 CL34 也足以应对这类轻量向量化负载。

知名爆料者 HXL 发现了 EPYC 9996 的 GeekBench 结果，俄罗斯爱好者“three twenty six”随后用 Ryzen 7 9700X 在相同 4.1GHz 频率下做了直接比较。Ryzen 7 9700X 是 8 核 Zen 5 桌面 CPU，配备 32MB L3，每核缓存比例与 EPYC 9996 相同，但本地缓存总量小得多。测试平台包括 Windows 11 和 CachyOS Linux；EPYC 9996 所在 Dell PowerEdge R9815 服务器的单线程得分为 2847，Ryzen 7 9700X 在 Linux 下为 2483、Windows 下为 2318。也就是说，GeekBench 单线程总分约高出 15%，但这一数字不能直接等同于“Zen 6 IPC 比 Zen 5 高 15%”。

从 Linux 分项结果看，EPYC 9996 相对桌面 Zen 5 芯片没有出现回退，且不同测试的领先幅度差异明显：HTML5 浏览器测试领先约 24%，这类测试通常对内存延迟敏感，可能受益于巨大的 L3 缓存；资产压缩领先 19%，视频编码领先 21%，照片编辑领先 17%，这些更可能反映 Zen 5 与 Zen 6 之间的真实架构差异。值得注意的是，Geekbench 历来对 CPU SIMD 利用较轻，该测试标记为 AVX2，并未使用两颗 CPU 都具备的 AVX-512 单元，因此结果更多衡量整数运算和内存子系统性能，而非纯粹的向量算力。这也让 Zen 6 在媒体处理等项目中表现突出显得更有意思。

不过，文章强调不能把这次结果当作定论，因为混杂因素很多。最重要的一点是，EPYC 9996 使用的是 Zen 6c 高密度核心，主打面积效率，牺牲了高频扩展能力，并不是未来桌面版 Zen 6 所用的核心；4.1GHz 在当今也算不上高频，尤其对于采用尖端 2nm 级工艺的芯片而言。真正值得期待的是：Zen 5 相对 Zen 4 的 IPC 提升有限，甚至出现部分回退，若 Zen 6 能带来显著 IPC 提升，并叠加传闻中的较大频率跃升，桌面平台可能迎来类似 Core 2 到 Core i7 那样的跨越。文章称 Zen 6 桌面产品已确认将登陆 AM5 平台，预计明年年初发布，届时内存供应能否跟上也成了调侃式的关注点。

history.title: Kevin Roose is AGI-pilled. Why aren’t you?
history.description:
Today, I’m talking to Kevin Roose, journalist and author of the new book The AGI Chronicles, which details the recent and explosive transformation of the AI industry.
Kevin was a longtime New York Times reporter and host of the popular podcast Hard Fork, but he and friend of the show Casey Newton just left the Times to start the all-new tech podcast Machine Gods, which launched last week.
Kevin and I talked about launching Machine Gods and what it’s like to go from The New York Times to being an independent creator — and then of course we talked about the book, which is an excellently reported dive into the companies racing to build artificial general intelligence.
I wanted to get a sense from Kevin of what it was like to report this, to try and understand these characters and this moment in time, and where it all goes next. Fair warning: This conversation takes a pretty philosophical turn at the end, but I think you’ll find it a really worthwhile back-and-forth.
Okay: Kevin Roose on The AGI Chronicles, starting Machine Gods, and where AI goes from here. Here we go.


This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
Kevin Roose, you are the author of The AGI Chronicles and the cofounder and cohost of the new podcast Machine Gods. Welcome to Decoder.
Thanks so much for having me.
I was listening to the first episode of Machine Gods and you and Casey discussed the fact that technically you have the title of CEO.
It’s true. I won the coin flip and we needed someone. When you start a company as we have, you need to list someone as the CEO, I guess, to know who to haul in front of Congress when our first scandal inevitably breaks. So that’s going to be me.
It’s funny because you’re a CEO on Decoder. It means I’m going to have to ask you the Decoder questions.
[Laughs] Okay. Well, I’ve been a CEO for about five minutes and most days I frankly forget I’m the CEO.
Honestly, that tracks with most of the CEOs on the show. They all act like they’ve only done it for five minutes. We’ll come to it.
I want to talk about your book. It’s called The AGI Chronicles. It is a meticulously reported book about the main frontier labs and the culture shift they’ve all undergone as AI has come into the forefront and become a much more commercial product in many ways.
But let’s just start with Machine Gods. You were a journalist for The New York Times for a long time. Obviously, I think the audience probably knows this, but you and I have known each other for a long time. I will say that since I have known you, your desire to be a YouTuber has been top of mind. You’re just like, “How do I get over there?” And I’ve always been like, “Run, don’t do it.” But you did it.
You left The Times, you started your own podcast with our friend Casey Newton. It is the next generation of the very popular podcast, Hard Fork, which was excellent. And I’m excited for you, but what made you take the leap?



Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here. 
Yeah, you have been trying to convince me out of this for as long as I’ve been trying to convince myself into it and you have not succeeded because here I am.
Yep, I failed. Utterly failed.
No, look, I think that for some very good reasons, media companies have long been a little bit wary of going all in on YouTube or any other video platform. The ones that have gone all in have not necessarily come out of that with good feelings about it because there are a lot of–
Yeah, they pivot to video and also into death, routinely.
Yeah, you pivot to video or you sort of waste a bunch of money doing things that don’t pay for themselves. So, I think there are some structural economic reasons for that, but I also think it’s that there aren’t a lot of institutions that are equipped to make that kind of a long-term bet.
I’ve been trying to YouTube-pill people in media for many years, as you know. You’ve been trying to undo the YouTube-pilling on your end, but I just think it’s clearly the most important media platform in the world right now. It’s a place where journalism has not historically had a central place.
If you were to look at YouTube as a whole and try to assess what piece of it is dedicated to what you or I would consider high-quality journalism, it’s a vanishingly small part of the overall ecosystem there.
So, part of my mission is just to crack that and figure out how to do YouTube and video in general in a way that is sustainable from an economic and a sort of creative standpoint. And then just to experiment and do a bunch of things.
This is not a face that needs to be on YouTube. So I’m also hoping to bring some other people in and nail some formats. But I look at what The Verge has done there. I look at what people like Joanna Stern and MKBHD have done there. To me, that is very exciting and it’s a space where there’s a lot less competition than text or podcasts.
Machine Gods is a podcast that you’re doing in partnership with NPR, which I want to talk about. But do you think of it as a YouTube product?
We want it to be video-first. What that means basically is that we are going to give a shit about what it looks like to a degree that we have not always done. We’re going to try to give people a lot of reasons to want to watch as well as listen.
Obviously, we know that there are some people who just don’t like video podcasts and so we want to give the audio audience something that is enjoyable, but this is the direction of things. You can’t do a podcast now without doing video on top of it. So we’re going to try to really embrace that and make a good version of it that is as good as two middle-aged journalists can pull off on YouTube.
Truly the future of media is middle-aged journalists pivoting to YouTube. I feel the same way because I’m now making more video and that’s what we’re doing. It’s going to be great.
The other reason to leave and to do this — and obviously people know I’m friends with Casey as well, and I’ve been talking to you and him about it for a long time — is that the AI story is here. There is a platform shift. There are new companies, new characters, new ideas to talk about in the world. It’s funny because in that context, usually you get a media shift as well. The way we tell stories or the formats we tell stories usually shifts alongside the thing we are talking about or the technology we’re talking about.
Here, YouTube feels like the most solid media foundation that exists. It’s the one that’s the same the most, even though it’s changing and it has YouTube Shorts and now you can A / B test everything, including your own face. But it’s the one that is the most the same. Instagram has undergone some massive change and it feels like that will continue happening.
Does it feel like YouTube is the most stable place to build as you’re trying to tell these new stories?
It does. I mean, obviously you never want to put all your eggs in one basket. So, we are also distributing video on Apple Podcasts and Spotify and we’re going to be everywhere. But yeah, it feels relatively stable.
The question I’m always wondering is what would it take to replace YouTube? Many companies have tried to replace YouTube, but to do that, you would not only have to build an experience that was better for creators and better for users, but you would also have to replicate the entire visual corpus of humanity. You would have to just get 6 million videos from plumbers about how to fix every individual sink and then upload it to that. It’s a really hard thing to displace. It is so ingrained for so many people, and I just think it’s going to keep growing.
We’ll come to this when we talk about AI, but a long time ago I asked Google CEO Sundar Pichai, “Well, what are you going to do if there’s no more websites?” And he was kind of like, “Well, we have YouTube.” And there’s just no arguing with that. You sure do. And it is just going to keep growing.
What has been the most surprising thing about going from The New York Times to what you might call the creator economy?
Well, we’re very new at it, but surprising to me so far is how much I like all the business stuff. I think in journalism, you’re always taught to stay in your lane, and I have never run a business before. Casey has run a business. I knew he enjoyed it. But for me, these are new muscles and I don’t enjoy all of it. Negotiating the insurance quotes for our defamation coverage is not what I would feel compelled by. But regarding actually running a business, there is something to this founder thing.
Yeah, it’s a good time. It’s funny, in talking to you and to Casey and Joanna, who also just left and started her own thing, that comes up a lot. From my perspective, it’s why I’ve been doing this a long time. What if I stopped running the business? That doesn’t seem to be a choice. This is the future of media — taking control of your business and taking control of your audience. There’s something very powerful there.
One of the things I want to talk about, and then I definitely want to talk about the book at length, is the audience for AI coverage, because I see it in two ways. There’s a group of people building the stuff that loves it and wants to consume all of it. There’s a group of people that truly hates it and thinks all of it is fake.
And then there’s what I would call an expanding group in the middle where the products have become more useful. You have to look at them and evaluate them as they are. They were not terribly useful a couple years ago. The promises did not match reality, but every day now it can do one more thing that it couldn’t do before. Whether that thing is hacking all of the websites in the world, we’ll set that aside, but AI can do things it couldn’t do before and the audience seems to be changing.
How are you thinking about the audience for Machine Gods and how it might grow or change?
I mean, right now we’re just trying a bunch of stuff that we think will be good and we hope that it will find its sort of natural audience. But I think you’re right that the audience is changing. I think for a while there was a lot of demand for cope — basically people telling you this is not happening, you don’t have to pay attention to it, it sucks, it’s hurting the environment.
There still is in some parts of the internet. YouTube has a weird amount of this still going on and Reddit is also very anti-AI. But I think most people, or at least maybe a plurality of people, are either resigned to or excited about the fact that this is not going away. That is the audience that we’re looking for.
We’re not trying to tell you that AI is amazing and we’re going to be in AI utopia under the new machine regime.
